sections.h2: Where is Charleston, SC, and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Charleston is the county seat of Charleston County and the most populous city in South Carolina. It sits on Charleston Harbor, which is formed by the Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers and runs about 7 miles southeast to the Atlantic.

The old downtown is known as the Peninsula, with the Ashley River on the west and the Cooper River on the east. The city limits also take in West Ashley, James Island, Johns Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island. A house on the Peninsula and a house on Johns Island share a city name but face very different rules, lot types and buyer pools.

sections.h2: What does Charleston's history mean for an older house?
sections.html:
Charleston has been settled for more than 340 years, so many houses here are old, and old houses come with repair lists. The city was founded in 1670, and by the 1690s it was among the five largest cities in North America.

Two events left marks on the building stock. An earthquake in 1886, estimated at magnitude 7.0, damaged about 2,000 buildings. Hurricane Hugo, a Category 4 storm on September 21, 1989, caused more than $2.8 billion in damage.

Neither event decides what your house is worth today. They do explain why buyers and inspectors in Charleston look closely at foundations, roofs, wiring and past water damage, and why a seller with deferred repairs may find a traditional listing slow.

Charleston's economy rests on tourism, port and logistics, aerospace and information technology. The Port of Charleston is one of the busiest in the country, and Boeing is a major aerospace employer.

The technology sector has grown enough to earn the nickname Silicon Harbor. Education adds to the mix: the College of Charleston and The Citadel are both in the city.

For a seller, this mix means demand comes from several directions at once: people relocating for jobs, investors, and buyers who want a second home near the water. It also means a house in the wrong condition or the wrong flood zone can be hard to place with an ordinary buyer who needs a mortgage.

sections.h2: How do hurricanes and flooding affect selling a house in Charleston?
sections.html:
Flood risk is the single biggest condition issue for many Charleston houses. The city sits at about 3 feet of elevation, summer is the wettest season with almost half of the annual rainfall falling from June through September, and hurricanes are a threat in summer and early fall.

The City of Charleston runs a floodplain program with rules that matter at sale time. Its Flood Zones page says any work inside a Special Flood Hazard Area needs a permit, including painting, interior finishes and storm-damage repairs. The Special Flood Hazard Area covers AE, Coastal A and VE zones, which have a 1 percent or greater annual chance of flooding.

The city's floodplain page lists these points for owners:

  • Since July 1, 2020, new construction in the flood hazard area must be designed 2 feet above Base Flood Elevation, and residential substantial improvements must be 1 foot above it.
  • Slab-on-grade building types 1A, 1B, 2A and 3 are prohibited in the 100-year floodplain for projects applied for on or after January 1, 2024.
  • Coastal A Zone design rules have applied to new construction and substantial improvements since January 1, 2023.
  • FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 applied to new flood policies from October 1, 2021 and to renewals from April 1, 2022.

Elevation certificates and flood hazard information can be requested from the city at floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. Ask for them before you set a price, because a buyer's flood insurance quote can change what they are willing to pay. See the city's floodplain management page and flood zone permit page.

sections.h2: Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Charleston house?
sections.html:
Only in limited cases. The city sorts short-term rentals into categories by location, and every category limits a property to one short-term rental unit.

  • Category 1 covers the Old and Historic District on the peninsula, for existing structures individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 covers the rest of the peninsula outside the overlay, for buildings constructed 50 or more years ago.
  • Category 3 covers areas off the peninsula, including Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

Each category requires one extra off-street parking space, 9 feet by 18 feet 6 inches, on top of the parking the zoning ordinance already requires. A single-family home needs 3 spaces in total. Commercially zoned property in the overlay can seek a Commercial Short Term Rental Permit, and residentially zoned property can seek a Bed and Breakfast Permit. Questions go to shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov or 843-724-7311. The details are on the city's category criteria page.

If your house has been used as a rental, tell buyers what permit it holds. A buyer paying for rental income will want proof.

sections.h2: What does it cost to transfer a deed in South Carolina?
sections.html:
The state deed recording fee is $1.85 for each $500 of value, or any part of $500, under South Carolina Code section 12-24-10. Of that, $1.30 goes to the state and $0.55 to the county.

The seller is the one liable, with the buyer secondarily liable. Taking a $300,000 sale as an example, there are 600 blocks of $500, so the fee works out to $1,110. A value affidavit is filed with the deed, and the register of deeds can waive it. Some transfers are exempt, including a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and the affidavit must then state the reason. The statutes are at scstatehouse.gov.

Charleston County sets its own recording and tax dates. We could not open the county auditor and assessor pages while writing this, so call those offices for the current reassessment notices, appeal dates and bill due dates before you plan a closing.

sections.h2: How is a house taxed in Charleston, and does that change when you sell?
sections.html:
South Carolina taxes an owner-occupied legal residence at a 4 percent assessment ratio, and other property at 6 percent. The 4 percent rate applies to the home and up to five contiguous acres, and the home cannot be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year.

A buyer who will not live in the house usually loses the 4 percent rate, so the same house can carry a larger bill after a sale to an investor. Counties must reassess property every fifth year, and owners must be notified of value changes of $1,000 or more (Code sections 12-43-217 and 12-43-220).

sections.h2: What do sellers in Charleston usually face?
sections.html:
Sellers here tend to run into the same few problems, and each one points to a different sale route.

  • Flood-zone repairs that need a permit before they can start.
  • Older structures with deferred roof, plumbing or electrical work.
  • Inherited houses that need heirs to agree before anything is signed.
  • Rental houses where the tenant, the permit or both need sorting out.

A listing suits a house that is in good shape and can wait for showings. A sale to a cash buyer suits a house where repairs, permits or a deadline make a long listing a poor fit. Whichever you choose, get the flood zone, the permit history and your payoff figure in hand first.

faqs.q: What is the main flood rule when I sell a house in Charleston?
faqs.a: The city requires a permit for any work in a Special Flood Hazard Area, including repairs after storm damage. Since July 1, 2020, residential substantial improvements there must sit 1 foot above Base Flood Elevation. Ask the floodplain office for your elevation certificate before you price the house.

faqs.q: How much is the South Carolina deed fee on a Charleston sale?
faqs.a: It is $1.85 per $500 of value, so a $300,000 sale carries a $1,110 fee. By statute the seller is liable and the buyer is secondarily liable. Your closing attorney will show the exact figure.

faqs.q: Can I rent my Charleston house short term after buying it?
faqs.a: Maybe. Each of the city's three categories allows one short-term rental unit per property and an extra parking space. Category 1 and 2 depend on location and building age on the peninsula. Confirm with the city before you count on rental income.

faqs.q: Does selling to a cash buyer change flood or permit duties?
faqs.a: No. Disclosure, permits and the deed fee apply however the house sells. A cash sale can skip buyer financing delays and repair requests, and that is the practical difference for most Charleston sellers.

faqs.q: Where can I find Charleston County tax dates?
faqs.a: Start with the county auditor, assessor and treasurer. South Carolina law sets January 15 as the last day to pay without penalty on most bills, but the county notices and appeal windows are specific to each cycle, so call the offices directly.
